pages.text: The Surprising Risks of Quitting Ozempic | National Geographic Premium HEALTH The Surprising Risks of Quitting Ozempic Weight regain is only part of the story. Scientists are discovering how stopping GLP-1 drugs may affect the heart, blood sugar, and other protective benefits that go well beyond the scale. GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro can reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. But new research raises questions about how much of that protection remains after patients stop taking the medications. Photo Illustration: NGM Staff; Source Photo: Rebecca Hale, National Geographic By Bethany Brookshire Published November 2, 2026 Most people know that when they start a prescription for GLP-1 receptor agonists—such as Ozempic or Mounjaro—they work over time and are a long-term treatment. Stop taking GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic or Mounjaro, and many people regain at least some of the weight they’ve lost. Blood sugar levels may rise again, too. But research suggests that stopping these medications may carry another, less obvious consequence: the loss of some of the drugs’ protections against heart attack and stroke. In a study of more than 132,000 U.S. veterans taking GLP-1 medications, researchers found that treatment offered cardiovascular benefits. But when people ceased the medications, their cardiovascular risks tended to rise. pages.text: The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies | National Geographic Premium ANIMALS The Surprising Secret Weapon Against Spotted Lanternflies Early research suggests that a backyard plant might poison the invasive species. Scientists are studying a promising way to control the spread of the invasive spotted lanternfly with a common plant. Mark Mirko, Connecticut Public/Getty Images By Jason Bittel Published September 1, 2026 The spotted lanternfly is a large, visually striking insect that first showed up in the U.S. in 2014. In just over a decade, this invasive species has multiplied across the American Northeast, with new range expansions into the Midwest and South, bringing the total number of states where they can now be found to 19, as well as the District of Columbia. Not only do they feed on plant sap and harm trees, but spotted lanternflies also pose a threat to the grape and wine industry , among many other crops. Scientists have recently said that squashing them likely won’t make a dent in their populations. However, they may have stumbled upon a new weapon in the fight against the invasive species—one that just so happens to be critical habitat for monarch butterflies , an insect species perhaps as loved as the lanternfly is despised: Milkweed. When spotted lanternflies feed on the stuff, they have a tendency to drop dead. “We were planning to run the experiment for a week, except when we went back the next day, the majority of the lanternflies that were on milkweed were dead,” says Anne Johnson , a postdoctoral researcher at Michigan State University.

pages.text: The surprising ways exercise helps the body fight cancer | National Geographic Premium HEALTH The surprising ways exercise helps the body fight cancer A landmark study suggests physical activity can help cancer patients live longer. Scientists are learning why. Exercise has long been recommended to help lower the risk of developing cancer. Now, growing evidence suggests it may also help reduce the risk of recurrence and improve survival after a diagnosis. Jose Luis Carrascosa Martínez, Alamy By Cathy Nelson Published June 9, 2026 For decades, doctors have recommended exercise to help cancer patients manage treatment side effects and improve their quality of life. But a landmark new study suggests exercise doesn’t just help cancer patients feel better—it may help keep cancer from returning. The 2025 CHALLENGE Trial , published in the New England Journal of Medicine , was the first large randomized controlled study to test whether a structured exercise program could improve long-term outcomes for colon cancer patients after they had completed surgery and chemotherapy. After a median follow-up of eight years, patients with stage 2 and 3 colon cancer who participated in the program had a 28 percent lower risk of disease recurrence, a new primary cancer, or death than those who received exercise education alone. They also had a 37 percent lower risk of death from any cause. According to the study authors, the magnitude of the survival benefit was similar to that seen with many approved cancer drug therapies. pages.text: The Teeth That Changed the Story of Human Evolution | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE FROM THE VAULT The Teeth That Changed the Story of Human Evolution In East Africa in the 1990s, Meave Leakey and the Hominid Gang discovered apelike creatures who walked upright four million years ago. Ape, hominid, or something in between? Based on the shape of the embedded tooth, some researchers believe that a 5.6-million-year-old jaw fragment discovered at Lothagam in 1967 is the oldest hominid fossil yet found. Skeptics say the fragment is too meager to classify. Other finds, in the 1970s, have been identified as specimens of the early hominid Australopithecus afarensis : a partial skeleton called Lucy from Hadar in Ethiopia and a 3.5-million year-old mandible from Tanzania exhumed by the author's mother-in-law, Mary Leakey. With the 1994 Turkana expedition the horizon was pushed back another 600,000 years. Meanwhile, research in Ethiopia by Tim White of the University of California, Berkeley, has uncovered even older fossils, which he has identified as a new genus, Ardipithecus . pages.text: The tree nobody liked | National Geographic By Rick Gore Photographs by Bianca Lavies Published April 9, 2026 This story originally published in the May 1977 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here . I still recall the dredges and the bulldozers working in the red mangrove swamps near my father's house. I never thought their destruction was much of a loss. Mangroves were scrub: junk trees. The peculiar aerial roots, which, like spidery legs, prop the mangroves up in the mud, made the swamps seem forbidding. Swarms of mosquitoes and clicking, crablike creatures lurked within. The mud often stank. "No one likes the mangroves," John Steinbeck once wrote. And in Florida, until very recently, he was right. Few people complained as stands of mangroves along the state's southeast coast were replaced with sea-walled housing developments, hotels, and shopping plazas. Today most of Florida's red mangroves are part of a lush fringe extending along the southern Gulf Coast. They embrace the Ten Thousand Islands, wrap around Everglades National Park, and reach to the tip of the Florida Keys. In the past few years the red mangrove has made a lot of friends. "It is the sacred tree of Florida," says Bill Merrihue of Naples, president of the Collier County Conservancy. Sacred enough for a Miami federal judge to order a trailer-park developer in the Keys to restore to its natural state a mangrove swamp he had dredged without proper permit. pages.text: The Volkswagen Beetle Says Auf Wiedersehen Skip to main content The VW Beetle is retiring Wikimedia /CC BY-SA 2.0 DE The last ever Volkswagen Beetle is rolling off the production line in Puebla, Mexico, today, before heading to go on display at a nearby Volkswagen museum, David McHugh at the Associated Press reports. While car models arrive and disappear each year (take, for instance, the Ford Fiesta , Chevy Cruze and Daimler’s all-electric Smart Car, all of which are also ending production in 2019), few vehicles traveled the long, strange road of the Beetle—often lovingly known as the Bug—which originated out of Nazi Germany and later came to personify the peace-and-love ethos of the 1960s. When Adolf Hitler became chancellor in 1933, he wanted to create a rugged, affordable automobile that would spread car ownership “to the people” throughout the German Reich. In 1938, he was poised to do so, as the Nazis geared up for the mass production of what was then known as the KdF-Wagen—an abbreviation of Kraft durch Freude , literally making it the "Strength Through Joy" car (the name was associated with a larger state-run leisure initiative ). But as the Nazi war machine ramped up, the project was tabled as the factory intended for car production was converted to make military vehicles instead. After the war, however, the factory outside Hanover was relaunched under civilian leadership in 1949 and the production of the car, rebranded as the Beetle, began. Maxime Aubert By Dyna Rochmyaningsih Published January 21, 2026 On Muna, a tropical island off southeastern Sulawesi, Indonesia, lies a cave decorated with prehistoric paintings. Locals call it Liang Metanduno. They visit the archaic art gallery to marvel at depictions of flying human figures, boats filled with passengers, and mounted warriors drawn with red, brown, and sometimes black pigment. In 2015, Adhi Agus Oktaviana, an archaeologist at Indonesia’s National Agency for Research and Innovation (BRIN), travelled to Liang Metanduno in search of a much older form of human artistic expression, one that predated the birds, pigs, and horses painted on its walls only a few thousand years ago. On the ceiling near a brown scribble of a chicken, Oktaviana found it: two hand stencils, one of which had a pointy finger like an animal claw. Gossett Jr., The New York Times/Redux By Melissa Sartore Published March 12, 2025 Virginia Allen was just 16 years old when she joined the nursing staff at Sea View Hospital in New York City, a facility that opened specifically to address the millions dying of tuberculosis, also called “consumption”. At the time, the highly contagious illness was poorly understood and many white healthcare workers refused to help. Allen was one of the thousands of Black nurses— the “Black Angels”—who stepped up, joining her aunt Edna Sutton Ballard at the Staten Island hospital. It was a “rich work experience [and] when I look back over all of those years, it has really been a phenomenal journey,” Allen remembers. “ They were phenomenal nurses… the relationship that those nurses fostered, they were like family. Each one helping the other." The Black Angels did more than simply provide medical care. They facilitated the development of a cure for tuberculosis, helped desegregate hospitals in New York, and fought a war against a disease that continues to kill millions of people worldwide annually. pages.text: There's a Critical Window in Your 50s for Preserving Body Strength | National Geographic Premium HEALTH There's a Critical Window in Your 50s for Preserving Body Strength The fight against frailty can begin decades before physical decline becomes obvious. A new study suggests that biological changes linked to frailty may accelerate at two particular ages in midlife. But researchers have uncovered ways to preserve strength and independence into the twilight years. Rebecca Hale, NGM Staff By Hadia Zainab Published November 4, 2026 Frailty may seem like a problem for old age. But the biological changes that make us more vulnerable to physical decline can begin decades before the first signs appear. A 2026 study in Cell Metabolism analyzed data from more than 50,000 people and found that changes in proteins associated with frailty clustered around two ages: roughly 50 and 63. These molecular patterns may help scientists understand how frailty develops before physical signs appear. Researchers also developed a protein-based frailty score that could eventually help identify people at risk, although more research is needed before it can be used clinically. Around age 50, many of the changes involved proteins related to how the body uses and stores energy and regulates hormones. Here's how they were rediscovered. | National Geographic By Carles Aguilar Published July 25, 2024 Lost cities sunken beneath the waves are not just myths. Many coastal communities were swallowed up by the sea in the ancient world—their streets, homes, and temples all submerged under relentless tides. For millennia legends swirled about these places, but their submarine statues made them impossible to explore in the field. Starting in the 20th century, breakthroughs in oceanography and marine science opened the door to underwater archaeology, allowing scholars to map sites, collect artifacts, and resurface the stories of these drowned cites. This bust of Neilos, god of the Nile, dates from 200 to 100 B.C. and was recovered from Canopus, Egypt. Christoph Gerigk. © /Franck Goddio/Hilti Foundation Some of humanity’s earliest coastal settlements met their fate because of climate change. Using geomorphological, sedimentological, and paleontological data from the seabed, scientists have established that between 30,000 and 20,000 years ago, during the last glacial maximum, sea level was some 425 feet lower than it is today. At the end of this period, the sea level rose abruptly as polar ice caps melted. Many prehistoric settlements built along the coastlines flooded and were abandoned. Often mistaken for fireflies or even worms, Orfelia fultoni are actually the glowing larvae of a fungus gnat. Measuring just 1.5 to 2 centimeters long, these translucent creatures emit bioluminescent blue light from both ends—and are most visible during late May to early June. Fireflies drift overhead, but the real spectacle is closer to the ground—an embankment where, nestled in damp moss, glowworms shine like pinpricks of neon blue. “They’re just so bright!” someone exclaims. A year later, an exhibit at the Brighton Museum & Art Gallery revealed the faces of seven more ancient “locals” who lived on the coast of southern England over the past 40,000 years, showing how science confirms that the history of the region is much more complicated than we once thought. pages.text: These Seabirds Are So Full of Plastic They’re Starving to Death | National Geographic ANIMALS These Seabirds Are So Full of Plastic They’re Starving to Death Researchers found one sable shearwater on Australia's Lord Howe Island with nearly 900 pieces of plastic in its stomach. In 2023, researchers found 403 plastic fragments in this sable shearwater's stomach. More recently, they found that one had swallowed 894 pieces of plastic. Justin Gilligan By Annie Roth Photographs by Justin Gilligan Published October 28, 2026 Just off Australia's eastern coast lies Lord Howe Island, a pristine paradise of white-sand beaches, vibrant coral reefs, and towering mountains. But on this island oasis, an ecological crisis is unfolding. The island’s iconic sable shearwaters are bursting with plastic. More than 75 percent of the island's sable shearwaters have plastic in their stomachs. When researchers pick up these birds, they hear hundreds of bottle caps, balloon clips, soy sauce packets, toothbrush heads, and plastic pellets (known as “nurdles”) rattling inside. “The birds are so completely full of plastic, from their esophagus all the way to their cloaca,” says Jennifer Lavers, a marine scientist with the Adrift Lab , a research cooperative focused on seabirds and marine plastic pollution. In some cases, the birds have so much waste inside that scientists can’t even get tubes down their throats. Much of what we assume about the 80-year-old body comes from people who stopped exercising decades ago. But these women rowers, whose average age is 80, defy those assumptions: They are poised to become the first women’s octogenarian eight to race the storied Head of the Charles regatta in October. The women push harder against their foot stretchers and gradually their movements begin to mirror one another as they find their rhythm—sliding their seats forward, dropping their blades into the water, and unleashing a collective push that drives the boat ahead. And this unusual crew of mostly silver-haired athletes is aiming to make history. pages.text: This ancient Greek warship ruled the Mediterranean | National Geographic By Arturo Sánchez Sanz Published February 23, 2023 • 13 min read Fast, maneuverable, and dangerous, the trireme was the most feared ship in ancient Greece. With powerful bronze rams and the ability to turn on a dime, it would leave enemy ships dead in the water by punching holes in their sides or smashing their oars. In his Histories , Herodotus writes how Greek naval dominance owed so much to the brilliant use of triremes in battle. ( This 3,500-year-old tomb held the treasures of Greece's 'Griffin Warrior'. ) In the fifth century B.C., Athenian shipyards had the capacity for over 300 triremes, the most famous warships of antiquity. The trireme—a term derived from the Greek trieres , “three rows of oars”—was the result of the continuous development of naval technology in the Greek world. The epic poem Iliad (attributed to Homer, and written in the eighth century B.C.) mentions ships called triaconters and penteconters , vessels that were crewed by 30 or 50 men, respectively. Biremes, with two rows of oarsmen, are recorded on eighth-century B.C. reliefs. At the beginning of the seventh century B.C., accumulated experience led to new technical advances, and the much more sophisticated trireme model appeared. Thucydides wrote that the Corinthians were the first to introduce the design to the Greek world, though modern historians think triremes may have first been built in Phoenicia, in the eastern Mediterranean and what is now Lebanon. Artwork By Craig Williams © The Trustees of the British Museum By Tom Metcalfe Published December 10, 2025 Archaeologists have discovered what may be the earliest evidence of deliberate fire-making. At a site called East Farm in England, recent excavations revealed reddened silt, flint handaxes distorted by heat, and fragments of a mineral—iron pyrite—that could have been used to make sparks on tinder. Taken together, the finds suggest that an early group of Neanderthals deliberately and repeatedly set fires in a hearth there roughly 400,000 years ago. While the several distinct pieces of evidence make a strong case, figuring out if early humans lit flames on purpose is hard because the archaeological traces of natural and human-made fires look very similar. NASA / James Blair On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days. Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission. The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks. “For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”

The dials turned smoothly, but only one of 1,296 possible combinations would open the device. The lock was an artifact from the Ann Francis , a merchant ship that sank in 1583. Hundreds of the vessel’s treasures—including compasses, coins and cannonballs—have since surfaced on the beach. But Hughes was particularly intrigued by the lock. It looked like a dinosaur vertebra at first. But upon further inspection, researchers realized the bone was a curved, sword-like crest that would have been attached to the skull of one of paleontology’s most oddball dinosaurs—the sail-backed predator Spinosaurus . “It was amazing,” recalls Vidal, of the University of Chicago. “It was like a unicorn.” Back in 2022, when he stumbled upon the strange bone, he was part of a team led by National Geographic Explorer Paul Sereno, a paleontologist also at Chicago , excavating a remote fossil site called Jenguebi. For centuries, the thermal springs have drawn visitors seeking healing, rest, and rejuvenation. Today, people come to soak in the water, drink it, and even sip beer brewed with it. After all, this is no ordinary water. What bubbles to the surface at Hot Springs National Park in Arkansas first fell as rain 4,000 years ago. Over the millennia, it seeped through thousands of feet of rock, warming as it went before faults and fractures in the sandstone channeled it back to the surface where now it gurgles up at 140° Fahrenheit. Long before Hot Springs was designated a national park in 1921, Native tribes, including the Caddo, Quapaw, and Osage, were drawn to its steaming waters.
